p: Acts is volume two. Volume one, addressed to the same Theophilus, is the Gospel of Luke.
b: The Greek says "the first account" (ton prōton logon). Both books are dedicated to Theophilus (Luke 1:3), and Acts picks up the story exactly where Luke's Gospel ends: the command to wait in Jerusalem and Jesus taken up (Luke 24:49–53). Ancient writers often began a second volume by summing up the first, as Josephus does in Against Apion 2.1. Classical Greek would use "former" for the first of two, and William Ramsay argued that "first" hints at a planned third volume; but in the Greek of Luke's day "first" was normal for "the earlier" of two, so most scholars draw no conclusion from it.
orig: τὸν μὲν πρῶτον λόγον (ton men prōton logon)

p: A real patron, probably of some rank, or a name for every reader who loves God.
b: Theophilos was a common Greek name meaning "friend of God" or "loved by God." Luke 1:3 calls him "most excellent" (kratiste), the title Acts gives the Roman governors Felix and Festus (Acts 23:26; 26:25). So most scholars think he was a real person of standing, perhaps a sponsor who paid for the book's copying, and perhaps a new believer who had been "taught" about Jesus (Luke 1:4). Origen and others read the name as a symbol: the book is for anyone who is a friend of God. Later guesses that he was a Roman official, or a high priest of that name, cannot be proved.

a: began to do and to teach
p: The word suggests that Acts tells what Jesus goes on doing and teaching through his followers.
b: "Began" can be a simple Greek idiom for "did" (Luke often uses it this way), but many readers since John Chrysostom have pressed it: the Gospel told what Jesus began, and Acts tells what the risen Jesus continues to do from heaven through the Spirit and the church. Acts supports this reading. Jesus pours out the Spirit (2:33), heals through his name (3:6, 16; 9:34, "Jesus Christ heals you"), adds people to the community (2:47) and appears to Stephen and Paul (7:56; 9:5).
orig: ἤρξατο ... ποιεῖν τε καὶ διδάσκειν (ērxato ... poiein te kai didaskein)

p: The verb is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for Elijah carried up to heaven.
b: Analambanō, "take up," is used for Elijah's departure in the Greek of 2 Kings 2:9–11 and in later books that remember it (Sirach 48:9; 1 Maccabees 2:58). Luke uses the noun, analēmpsis, at the turning point of his Gospel: "As the days were coming to completion before he would be taken up" (Luke 9:51), and the verb again at 1:11 and 1:22. The Elijah story matters here: Elisha receives a share of Elijah's spirit because he sees him taken up, "If you see me being taken from you, then you will have it" (2 Kings 2:10). In Acts the disciples watch Jesus go, and then receive the Spirit (1:9; 2:4).
orig: ἀνελήμφθη (anelēmphthē)

t: Through the Spirit: orders or choosing?
p: The Greek can tie the Spirit to Jesus' orders or to his choosing of the apostles.
b: The phrase stands between "having given orders to the apostles" and "whom he had chosen," and it can go with either. Most translations, like this one, attach it to the orders: the risen Jesus instructs his apostles through the Spirit. Others attach it to the choosing, which Luke 6:12–13 says Jesus did after a night of prayer. Either way, Acts begins as it will go on, with the Holy Spirit named in its second verse; the Spirit appears about sixty times in the book.
orig: διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου (dia pneumatos hagiou)

p: A technical word for evidence that settles a question, used by Greek orators and doctors.
b: Tekmērion appears only here in the New Testament. Aristotle's Rhetoric uses it for a proof that is conclusive, as opposed to a mere sign, and medical writers used it for a symptom that settles a diagnosis. Luke's word fits his promise to Theophilus to give "certainty" (Luke 1:4). The proofs he means are the meals, the touching and the teaching of Luke 24:36–43; in 10:41 Peter says the witnesses ate and drank with the risen Jesus. Readers who doubt the bodily resurrection reply that "proofs" here are the claims of the witnesses, which the reader must weigh.
orig: ἐν πολλοῖς τεκμηρίοις (en pollois tekmēriois)

p: Only Acts gives the forty days. Luke's Gospel seems to tell the ascension on Easter evening.
b: Read alone, Luke 24 runs from the empty tomb to the ascension without a break, as if all happened on one day (Luke 24:1, 13, 33, 36, 50–51). Acts says Jesus appeared over forty days. Harmonizing view: the Gospel compresses the story, as ancient summaries often did, and Acts gives the fuller account; Paul too lists appearances spread over time (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). Literary view: forty is a Bible number for a time of preparation, Moses on the mountain (Exodus 24:18), Elijah's journey (1 Kings 19:8), Jesus in the wilderness (Luke 4:2), so Luke may use it as a round, meaningful number. The church keeps Ascension Day on the fortieth day after Easter.

t: Acts begins and ends with the kingdom
p: The risen Jesus teaches about God's kingdom, and the book's last verse has Paul doing the same.
b: "The kingdom of God" frames the whole book: Jesus speaks of it here, and in the last verse Paul is "proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ" in Rome (28:31; see also 8:12; 14:22; 19:8; 20:25; 28:23). So the apostles' preaching about Jesus is not a new subject: it is the same message of God's reign that Jesus preached in the Gospel, now centered on the risen king.

p: A rare verb: literally "taking salt together," or, in another spelling, "gathering" or "staying."
b: Synalizomenos is a rare word. If it comes from hals, "salt," it means "eating with them," which matches Luke 24:41–43 and Acts 10:41, and so the old Latin and Syriac translations and many modern ones read it. If it is a form of synaulizomai (some manuscripts spell it that way), it means "staying with them"; and a third derivation gives "gathering them together." Each fits the scene. Eating together was one of the proofs that Jesus was not a ghost.
orig: συναλιζόμενος (synalizomenos)

p: Jesus means the Holy Spirit, promised by the prophets and by Jesus himself.
b: The phrase repeats Luke 24:49, where Jesus says he is sending "the promise of my Father" and tells the disciples to stay in the city "until you are clothed with power from on high." The prophets had promised that God would pour out his Spirit in the last days: "On your children I will pour out my Spirit" (Isaiah 44:3; compare Isaiah 32:15; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28). Peter will say that the promise has now been kept (2:33, 39).

p: John's promise (Luke 3:16) now comes due. Christians differ on what this baptism is.
b: John the Baptist had said the one coming after him would baptize "in the Holy Spirit and fire" (Luke 3:16; Matthew 3:11). Jesus repeats the promise, and Peter will recall it at the house of Cornelius (11:16). In Acts, "baptized in the Spirit" names what happens at Pentecost (2:4: "filled"). Pentecostal teaching reads it as an empowering for witness that comes after conversion, with speaking in tongues as its first sign. Most other traditions read it as the gift of the Spirit that every believer receives in coming to Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13), with later "fillings" for particular tasks (4:8, 31). See the card on chapter 2.

a: giving the kingdom back to Israel
p: Was the disciples' question a mistake, or a true hope that Jesus left open?
b: The verb apokathistēmi is the word for restoring Israel in the prophets (Malachi 4:6 and Jeremiah 16:15 in the Greek), and the hope of a free Israel under a king of David's line was alive (Psalms of Solomon 17; Luke 1:32–33, 68–75; 24:21). The disciples misunderstood: Calvin wrote that their question had as many errors as words, and many readers think Jesus redirects them from a political kingdom to a worldwide spiritual one. A true hope, postponed: others note that Jesus corrects only the timing (1:7), and Peter still looks for "the restoring of all things" (3:21); Jacob Jervell and many recent scholars, and dispensationalists, read Acts as keeping a future for Israel. Fulfilled in the mission: a third view sees Israel restored as the Twelve gather Jews from every nation (Acts 2) and then the Gentiles (Isaiah 49:6).
orig: ἀποκαθιστάνεις τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ Ἰσραήλ (apokathistaneis tēn basileian tō Israēl)
r: Luke 1:32–33; Luke 24:21; Psalms of Solomon 17:21–32; Isaiah 49:6; 3:21; 15:16–17

p: Two Greek words: lengths of time, and the right moments. Neither is for the disciples to know.
b: Chronos is time as a span; kairos is the fitting moment. The pair was a common way to speak of the end (Daniel 2:21 in the Greek; 1 Thessalonians 5:1). Jesus does not deny that the kingdom will come; he says the date belongs to the Father, as in Matthew 24:36, where the Father alone knows "that day and hour." Instead of a timetable the disciples get a task: witness in the power of the Spirit (1:8).
orig: χρόνους ἢ καιρούς (chronous ē kairous)

p: "Witness" is the key word of Acts. In later Greek the same word came to mean "martyr."
b: Martys is a witness in court, someone who tells what he has seen. The apostles are witnesses of the resurrection (1:22; 2:32; 3:15; 5:32; 10:39–41), and so, later, are Stephen and Paul (22:15, 20; 26:16). Isaiah had God call Israel "my witnesses" before the nations (Isaiah 43:10, 12; 44:8), and that may stand behind Jesus' words. Because many witnesses died for their testimony, beginning with Stephen (22:20), the word came to mean "martyr" in the church of the second century.
orig: μου μάρτυρες (mou martyres)

a: as far as the farthest end of the earth
t: To the end of the earth: the plan of Acts
p: The phrase comes from Isaiah 49:6 and maps out the book: Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the world.
b: Isaiah's servant is made "a light to the nations" so that God's salvation may reach "to the farthest end of the earth" (Isaiah 49:6), and Paul quotes that verse in Acts 13:47. Acts follows the order of this verse: Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–9), and then, beginning with Cornelius and Antioch, the wider world (10–28). Where is "the end of the earth"? Some say Rome, where the book ends; the Psalms of Solomon 8:15 speaks of the Roman general Pompey as coming "from the end of the earth." Others point to the Ethiopian of chapter 8, from what Greeks thought the edge of the world, or read it as all nations without limit.

t: Taken up in a cloud: Romulus and others
p: Greek and Roman stories told of heroes carried up to the gods. Luke stresses eyewitnesses instead.
b: Roman legend said that Romulus, Rome's founder, vanished in a storm cloud and became a god; Livy tells it, with the rumor that the senators had killed him, and a senator later claimed to have seen him descending from heaven (Livy 1.16). Heracles and the deified emperors had similar stories. Some critical scholars (Gerhard Lohfink, Richard Pervo) think Luke shaped his scene with such accounts in mind, to show his Greek readers who the true exalted Lord is. Others note the differences: Luke's model is Elijah, not a pagan hero, and his story stresses sober witnesses watching in daylight ("while they looked on," "their eyes"), not a vanishing explained afterward. A real link of form is possible; a borrowing of belief is not likely.

p: In the Bible a cloud often shows God's presence: at Sinai, in the tabernacle, at the transfiguration.
b: The LORD led Israel "in a pillar of cloud" (Exodus 13:21), and his glory filled the tabernacle in a cloud (Exodus 40:34). At the transfiguration a cloud covers Jesus and the voice speaks from it (Luke 9:34–35). In Daniel's vision "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13), and Jesus said the Son of Man would come "in a cloud, with power and much glory" (Luke 21:27). So the cloud here is not weather: it marks Jesus being received into God's presence, and it points ahead to his return (1:11).
orig: νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτόν (nephelē hypelaben auton)
r: Exodus 13:21; Exodus 40:34; Luke 9:34–35; Daniel 7:13; Luke 21:27; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Revelation 1:7

p: Was it a literal rising into the sky, or a picture of Jesus' exaltation told in ancient terms?
b: Literal: most Christians through history, and all the creeds, read Luke as reporting a bodily, visible departure, the last appearance of the risen Jesus. Accommodated: many who accept it as an event add that its form was a sign suited to the witnesses; Pope Benedict XVI wrote that the ascension is not a journey into space but Jesus' entry into God's presence, made visible. Symbolic: Rudolf Bultmann and others held that a three-story universe stands behind "up," and that the scene is a mythical way of saying Jesus reigns with God. The rest of the New Testament speaks of Jesus' exaltation often but describes the departure scene only in Luke-Acts.

p: The same pair as at the empty tomb, and at the transfiguration: heavenly messengers who explain.
b: At the tomb "two men" in dazzling clothes ask the women why they look for the living among the dead (Luke 24:4–7). At the transfiguration "two men," Moses and Elijah, talk with Jesus about his "departure" (Luke 9:30–31). Luke uses the same wording for this scene, so the resurrection, the transfiguration and the ascension frame each other. White clothing marks heavenly beings (Daniel 7:9; Mark 16:5; Revelation 3:5). Two witnesses were what the Law required to confirm a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15).

p: One Greek word, ouranos, means both. It appears four times in this verse.
b: Greek, like Hebrew, has a single word for the sky above and for heaven, God's dwelling. This translation says "sky" in 1:10–11 because the scene is about what the disciples see; but the reader should hear both meanings, as the first readers did. The messengers' gentle rebuke has a point: the right response to the ascension is not to keep staring upward, but to go back to the city and wait for the Spirit, as the disciples do (1:12).
orig: εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν (eis ton ouranon)

p: The promise of Jesus' return. Readers differ on what "the same way" includes.
b: The messengers stress that it is "this same Jesus" (houtos ho Iēsous) who will come houtōs, "this same way." He will come houtōs ... hon tropon, "in the same manner" as he went. Most Christians read this as a personal, bodily and visible return, with clouds (Luke 21:27; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7), and the Mount of Olives, where he left, is where Zechariah 14:4 places the LORD's feet on the day of the LORD. Some take "the same way" more loosely: as he went in a cloud, the sign of God's presence, so he will return in divine glory. Preterist readers, who think most end-time prophecy was fulfilled in AD 70, usually still read this verse of a future return.
orig: οὕτως ἐλεύσεται ὃν τρόπον (houtōs eleusetai hon tropon)

p: The ridge east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron Valley, where Luke places the ascension.
b: Acts says the Mount of Olives, and Luke 24:50 says Jesus led them "as far as Bethany," a village on its eastern slope, so the two agree. Luke's Greek calls it "the mount called Olive Grove" (Elaiōn), as in Luke 19:29 and 21:37. The place had prophetic weight: Zechariah saw the LORD standing on it on the day he comes to fight for Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:4). From the 300s pilgrims honored the place: Eusebius says Constantine's mother Helena built a church on the mount, and later in that century a round shrine was built to mark the spot of the ascension.

a: as far as a person may walk on the Sabbath
p: About 2,000 cubits, roughly half to two-thirds of a mile: the limit Jewish teachers set for Sabbath travel.
b: Exodus 16:29 tells Israel not to go out from their place on the Sabbath. Jewish teachers set the limit at 2,000 cubits (about 1,000 yards, or 900 meters) beyond one's town, drawing on the 2,000-cubit pasture land around the Levites' towns (Numbers 35:5); the rule is spelled out in the Mishnah, tractate Eruvin. Luke uses the measure the way a Jewish reader would, as a sign that the place was close. Josephus gives the distance from Jerusalem to the Mount of Olives as five or six stadia, about the same.

p: A large upper room, probably in a private house. Tradition links it with the Last Supper.
b: The hyperōon was the upper story of a house, often the largest room, used for guests and gatherings (9:37; 20:8). Luke calls the room of the Last Supper by a different word (Luke 22:12), so he does not say it is the same place, though many have assumed it. Some guess it was the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where believers later met to pray (12:12). A building on Mount Zion called the Cenacle has been honored as the site since the 300s or earlier; the present room is from the Crusader period.

p: Luke's title for the Simon whom Matthew and Mark call "the Cananaean," from the Aramaic for "zealous."
b: Luke translates the Aramaic qan'ana, which Matthew 10:4 and Mark 3:18 keep as "Cananaean." A "zealot" could be anyone zealous for God's law, like Phinehas (Numbers 25:11) or Paul (22:3). Josephus uses "Zealots" for a revolutionary party in the war against Rome in AD 66–70, which formed decades later, so Simon may not have been a rebel; but he may have shared their passion. Either way, the Twelve held a tax agent for Rome, Matthew, and a man known for zeal.
orig: Σίμων ὁ ζηλωτής (Simōn ho zēlōtēs)

p: The Greek says only "Judas of James." The KJV took it as "brother of James."
b: Greek often names a man by the genitive of his father: "Judas of James" normally means "son of James," as here and in Luke 6:16. The KJV made him "brother of James" to identify him with Jude, who calls himself "brother of James" (Jude 1:1). In Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18 his place in the list is taken by "Thaddaeus," and most think the same man had two names. He appears once more by name in John 14:22, "Judas (not Iscariot)."
orig: Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου (Ioudas Iakōbou)

a: Mary, the mother of Jesus, and his brothers
p: Mary's last appearance in the New Testament, praying with the church. The brothers who once doubted now believe.
b: This is the last time Mary is named in the Bible. Luke places her among the praying disciples before Pentecost, as she was present at the start of the Gospel when the Spirit came on her (Luke 1:35). The brothers did not believe in him during his ministry, "not even his brothers were putting their faith in him" (John 7:5); after the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), they are with the church, and James later leads it (12:17; 15:13; 21:18). Who the brothers were, sons of Mary, sons of Joseph by an earlier wife, or cousins, is discussed on the topic page.

p: A favorite word of Acts: to keep at something with persistence.
b: Proskartereō means to hold fast to something, to persist. Luke uses it for the community's prayer here, for the four marks of the church in 2:42, for daily temple worship in 2:46, and for the apostles' work of "prayer and the ministry of the word" in 6:4. Before each great step in Luke-Acts there is prayer: Jesus' baptism (Luke 3:21), the choosing of the Twelve (Luke 6:12), and now the coming of the Spirit. "With one mind" (homothymadon) is another word Luke likes (2:46; 4:24; 5:12).
orig: προσκαρτεροῦντες ὁμοθυμαδὸν τῇ προσευχῇ (proskarterountes homothymadon tē proseuchē)

p: Twelve times ten. A later Jewish rule made 120 men the minimum for a town to have its own council.
b: The number may simply be what Luke knew. But readers have noticed that it is ten for each of the Twelve, and that the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 1:6) says a town needs 120 men to have a lesser Sanhedrin, its own court; if that rule is old, the group was large enough to act as a community. The Greek calls it "a crowd of names," an idiom for persons (Revelation 3:4). It is not the whole number of believers: Paul says the risen Jesus appeared to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:6).

a: what the Scripture said had to come true
p: The little Greek word dei, "it is necessary," runs through Luke-Acts: things happen by God's plan.
b: Edei, "it was necessary," is a mark of Luke's writing. The Messiah "had to" suffer (Luke 24:26), everything written about him "must" be fulfilled (Luke 24:44), Paul "must" see Rome (19:21; 23:11; 27:24). Peter applies this to Judas: even the betrayal fell within what Scripture foretold. He also says the Holy Spirit spoke "through the mouth of David," the early church's way of reading the Psalms as prophecy (2:30; 4:25).
orig: ἔδει πληρωθῆναι τὴν γραφήν (edei plērōthēnai tēn graphēn)

p: The Greek word for "share" is the word for a lot. It sets up the casting of lots in 1:26.
b: Klēros means a lot used for choosing, and then the portion that a lot assigns, such as a family's land in Joshua. Judas "obtained the lot" of this service: he was assigned his place. Peter's choice of word prepares for the lots of 1:26, where the place Judas left is reassigned. The Byzantine text uses klēros again in 1:25 (KJV "that he may take part of this ministry"); see the variant there.
orig: ἔλαχεν τὸν κλῆρον (elachen ton klēron)

a: this man came to own a piece of land
p: Matthew says Judas returned the money and hanged himself; Acts says he acquired land and fell. How do they fit?
b: In Matthew, Judas throws the silver into the sanctuary: "Then he went and hanged himself" (Matthew 27:5); the chief priests buy the Potter's Field with the money, and it is called the Field of Blood. In Acts, Judas himself "acquires" a plot with his pay, falls, and bursts open, and the place is called Field of Blood. Harmonizing view: an old explanation says he hanged himself and the body later fell and burst, and the priests bought the field in his name with his money. Critical view: most scholars think two independent traditions explained the name of a known place called Akeldama, each in its own way, each linked to Scripture (Zechariah 11:12–13 and Jeremiah in Matthew; the Psalms here). Both agree on a field bought with blood money, its name, and a shameful death.

p: The Greek prēnēs genomenos usually means "falling headlong"; some read "becoming swollen."
b: Prēnēs normally means "face down, headlong," and so the old translations read it. Some scholars proposed a rare medical sense, "swollen," because the bishop Papias (early 100s) told a gruesome story of Judas' body swelling until he burst; that story is preserved in later writers. The ordinary meaning fits the verb that follows: he "burst open in the middle." The language echoes the end of the wicked in Wisdom of Solomon 4:19, who are thrown "headlong" and burst.
orig: πρηνὴς γενόμενος (prēnēs genomenos)

p: Verses 18–19 are Luke's aside to Theophilus. Peter would not explain Aramaic to Aramaic speakers.
b: Peter's hearers lived in Jerusalem and spoke Aramaic, so "in their own speech" and the translation "meaning Field of Blood" are written for Greek readers. That is why most editions, like this one, put 1:18–19 in parentheses: Luke breaks into Peter's speech to tell what happened to Judas, then Peter goes on with the Scripture (1:20). The word for "speech," dialektos, returns at Pentecost, where each visitor hears his "own native language" (2:6, 8).
orig: τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν (tē idia dialektō autōn)

p: Aramaic haqel dema, "field of blood." Tradition places it in the Hinnom Valley south of Jerusalem.
b: The Greek spelling Hakeldamach renders Aramaic ḥaqel dĕmā', "field of blood"; the final "-ch" is a Greek way of marking a final Aramaic sound, also seen in names like Sirach. Since the 300s pilgrims have been shown a site on the southern slope of the Hinnom Valley, where Jeremiah broke a potter's jar (Jeremiah 19:1–2, 10–11) and where many rock-cut tombs of the Second Temple period have been found, fitting a burial ground for strangers (Matthew 27:7).

a: Let his farmstead be left empty
p: Peter joins Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8, psalms of a righteous sufferer betrayed by friends.
b: Psalm 69 is a lament the early church read as a prayer of Jesus; John 2:17 and 15:25 quote it. Its curse is plural in the Psalm, "Let their encampment be a ruin, with no one living in their tents" (Psalm 69:25), and Peter makes it singular for Judas. Psalm 109 is a prayer against a friend who repaid love with hatred: "Let another man take over his charge" (Psalm 109:8). Peter reads the first verse as describing Judas' deserted field and the second as a command to fill his place. In their own setting both are David's prayers against his enemies; Jewish readers take them so, and the early church read them as foreshadowing the betrayer.

p: The Greek episkopē means oversight or office. The KJV says "bishoprick."
b: The Greek Psalm uses episkopē, "oversight, office," from the same root as episkopos, "overseer," which became the word for a bishop (20:28; 1 Timothy 3:1). The KJV's "his bishoprick let another take" reflects that later sense. In the Psalm it means simply the man's position, and Peter applies it to Judas' place among the Twelve. Readers have drawn from it the idea of an office that continues when the holder changes; see the card on the chapter page.
orig: τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν αὐτοῦ (tēn episkopēn autou)

t: What makes an apostle, in Luke
p: For Luke, one of the Twelve must have been with Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension.
b: Peter's rule sets the limits of the Twelve: men who saw the whole of Jesus' public life and the risen Lord. By this rule Paul could not be one of the Twelve, and Acts almost never calls him an apostle (only 14:4, 14, with Barnabas). Paul himself insists that he is an apostle because he saw the risen Lord and was sent by him (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8–9; Galatians 1:1). The Twelve's task is to be witnesses (1:8), and the number matters because they stand for the twelve tribes of Israel (Luke 22:30).

p: The candidate not chosen. Papias later told a story about him surviving poison.
b: He had three names, as many Jews of the time did: a Hebrew name (Joseph), an Aramaic family name (Barsabbas, "son of the Sabbath" or "son of Sabba"), and a Latin name for dealing with the Roman world (Justus). Another Barsabbas, Judas, appears in 15:22. Eusebius reports that Papias told of Justus Barsabbas drinking deadly poison and suffering no harm by the Lord's grace (Church History 3.39.9). Nothing more is known of Matthias either; later traditions about his mission differ.

p: One Greek word, kardiognōstēs. The prayer may be addressed to Jesus, who chose the apostles.
b: Kardiognōstēs appears only here and in 15:8, where it is used of God. Scripture often says that God sees the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). Here "Lord" may be God, as in 15:8, or Jesus, since he is the one who "had chosen" the apostles (1:2) and the prayer asks which one "you have picked." If it is Jesus, the first recorded prayer of the church after the ascension is addressed to him, as Stephen's last prayer will be (7:59–60).
orig: καρδιογνῶστα (kardiognōsta)

a: to go to his own place
p: A grim phrase for Judas' end, usually read as his place of judgment.
b: The prayer contrasts two places: the "place" of service Judas left, and "his own place" to which he went. Early Christian writers use the same idiom: 1 Clement 5:4 says Peter went to the place of glory due to him, and Ignatius warns that each person will go to his own place (To the Magnesians 5:1). Most readers take it as Judas' place of judgment; others as simply his death, or his own chosen way. Acts does not say more, and it does not explain Judas' motives.
orig: πορευθῆναι εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν ἴδιον (poreuthēnai eis ton topon ton idion)

a: They handed out lots for them
p: The last time the Bible shows God's people deciding by lot. After Pentecost, Acts never uses it again.
b: Israel used lots to divide the land, to choose the goat on the Day of Atonement and to assign priestly duties (Luke 1:9), trusting that "every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). The apostles first narrow the field by human judgment, then pray, then leave the choice to God. Probably names were written on stones shaken in a container until one fell out. After the Spirit comes, decisions in Acts are made by the Spirit's guidance, prayer and the church's discussion (6:3–6; 13:2; 15:28). Some later Christians, such as the Moravians, still used lots; most churches have not.

a: he was counted in with the eleven apostles
p: Some have argued the apostles moved too fast and that Paul was God's twelfth apostle. Most disagree.
b: Matthias is never mentioned again, and some preachers and commentators have argued that the apostles acted before the Spirit came, and that Jesus' own choice for the empty place was Paul. Most interpreters reject this: Luke tells the story with approval, Peter acts on Scripture, the church prays, and the Twelve are restored to their full number before Pentecost, when they stand to speak to all Israel (2:14). Paul never claims to be one of the Twelve (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The verb synkatepsēphisthē, "was counted in," literally "voted in with pebbles," has also been taken to mean a vote followed the lot.
orig: συγκατεψηφίσθη (synkatepsēphisthē)

p: The harvest festival fifty days after Passover. Later Jewish tradition linked it with the giving of the Law at Sinai.
b: Pentēkostē means "fiftieth": the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot) came seven weeks after the first sheaf of the barley harvest, "Count fifty days, up to the day after the seventh Sabbath" (Leviticus 23:16). It was one of the three pilgrim feasts, so Jerusalem was full of visitors (2:5–11). The book of Jubilees, from the 100s BC, makes it the feast of covenant renewal, and the Talmud later calls it the day the Torah was given (Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 68b), since Israel reached Sinai in the third month (Exodus 19:1). Many readers see Luke drawing on that link: as the Law was given at Sinai, so the Spirit is given to God's people. Luke himself does not say so.
orig: τὴν ἡμέραν τῆς πεντηκοστῆς (tēn hēmeran tēs pentēkostēs)

p: Luke's verb is "was being fulfilled," the word he used when Jesus set out for Jerusalem.
b: Symplēroō means "to fill up completely." Luke uses it three times: twice of time, when the days before Jesus would be taken up were coming to completion and he set his face toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and here; and once of a storm filling a boat with water (Luke 8:23). The word suggests more than a date on the calendar: the day God had appointed has arrived, and the Father's promise (1:4) is about to be kept.
orig: ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι (en tō symplērousthai)

p: In Hebrew and Greek one word can mean wind, breath and spirit. The sound is like wind; the gift is the Spirit.
b: Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma both mean wind, breath and spirit, and Luke uses a near word, pnoē, "blowing." The Spirit as wind or breath runs through Scripture: God's breath gives Adam life (Genesis 2:7), the breath comes from the four winds to the dry bones of Ezekiel 37:9–14, and Jesus tells Nicodemus "The wind blows where it wants to" (John 3:8). Wind and fire together also marked God's coming at Sinai (Exodus 19:16–19) and to Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:11–12). Luke is careful: it was a sound "like" wind, and tongues "like" fire.
orig: ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας (hōsper pheromenēs pnoēs biaias)
r: Genesis 2:7; Ezekiel 37:9–14; John 3:8; John 20:22; Exodus 19:16–19; 1 Kings 19:11–12

p: Fire marks God's presence, as at Sinai and the burning bush. John promised a baptism in Spirit and fire.
b: At Sinai "the LORD had come down upon it in the fire" (Exodus 19:18). John the Baptist promised that the one coming would baptize "in the Holy Spirit and fire" (Luke 3:16). Jewish writers of the time told the Sinai story with fiery speech: Philo says the divine voice came out of the fire, the flame becoming speech the people could understand (On the Decalogue 46), and a later rabbinic tradition says each word from Sinai split into the seventy languages of the nations (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 88b). Whether or not Luke knew such traditions, readers who did would see Sinai here. The flame "parting" so that one rests on each person shows that the Spirit comes on every believer, not only on leaders.

t: Other languages: known tongues or ecstatic speech?
p: The Greek glōssa means both "tongue" and "language." Luke says the crowd heard their own native languages.
b: The same word glōssa is "tongues" of fire in 2:3 and "languages" here; this translation says "languages" because Luke explains that each visitor heard his own (2:6, 8, 11). Known languages (xenolalia): most readers through history, from Irenaeus on, have taken it as a miracle of speaking real foreign languages. A miracle of hearing: Gregory of Nazianzus discussed whether the miracle was in the speakers or in the hearers, and some still think the disciples spoke in tongues that each hearer understood in his own language. Ecstatic speech: many critical scholars think Luke has reworked memories of the ecstatic speech Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 14, which needs an interpreter, and note that some hearers thought them drunk (2:13). See the topic page.
orig: λαλεῖν ἑτέραις γλώσσαις (lalein heterais glōssais)

p: An unusual verb, used for the solemn speech of sages and prophets. Peter uses it in 2:14.
b: Apophthengomai means to speak out clearly and boldly. The Greek Old Testament uses it for prophets and for inspired speech (1 Chronicles 25:1; Ezekiel 13:9; Micah 5:12), and Greek writers for the sayings of wise men. Luke repeats it when Peter "spoke out" to the crowd (2:14) and when Paul answers Festus with words of truth and good sense (26:25). The point is that the Spirit gives not only power but speech: the first result of Pentecost is people speaking about God.
orig: ἀποφθέγγεσθαι (apophthengesthai)

a: from every nation in the whole world
p: By Jesus' time Jews lived across the Roman and Parthian worlds. Many came back to Jerusalem to live or for the feasts.
b: Luke says these Jews were "living" in Jerusalem (katoikountes), so many were Jews of the dispersion who had settled in the holy city, perhaps to die there, as well as pilgrims for the feast. Philo, writing about AD 40, lists Jewish settlements from Babylon and Persia to Egypt, Libya, Asia Minor, Greece and the islands (On the Embassy to Gaius 281–282), much like Luke's list. Greek writers spoke of "every nation under heaven" as a way of saying "the whole world" (compare Deuteronomy 2:25).

p: The verb is the one the Greek of Genesis 11 uses for the confusing of languages at Babel.
b: At Babel God said, "let us go down and mix up their language," and "the LORD mixed up the speech of all the earth" (Genesis 11:7–9); the Greek Old Testament uses syncheō, "confuse," the verb Luke uses here for the crowd. Many interpreters, from the church fathers on, read Pentecost as Babel reversed: there, languages divided humanity; here, the Spirit makes one message understood in many languages. Luke does not say this outright, and the languages are not abolished but used. This is an interpretation, though an old and widely held one; the list of nations in Genesis 10 may also stand behind 2:9–11.
orig: συνεχύθη (synechythē)

a: every one of these men talking is from Galilee
p: Galileans had a recognizable accent and were not known as learned or as linguists.
b: Matthew notes that Peter's Galilean speech gave him away: "The way you talk shows it" (Matthew 26:73). Later rabbinic tradition mocked Galileans for mispronouncing Aramaic (Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 53a–b). The crowd's surprise is not that Galileans can speak, but that these plain men from the north are speaking the languages of the far east and west. Compare 4:13, where the council sees that Peter and John have had no schooling.

a: We are Parthians, Medes and Elamites
p: About fifteen peoples and lands, running from Persia in the east to Rome in the west. Why these?
b: The list starts beyond the Roman Empire (Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamia, where many Jews had lived since the exile), moves through Asia Minor, Egypt and North Africa, and ends with Rome, Crete and Arabia. Three puzzles: Judea seems odd in a list of foreign lands, so some early writers read another name (Tertullian has Armenia) and modern scholars have guessed Syria or Idumea; but the Greek manuscripts agree on Judea. Elamites had long since ceased to be a nation, so the list may be old or literary. Its source: Stefan Weinstock compared it to an ancient astrological list of lands under the signs of the zodiac; others to Genesis 10, the table of the nations; others think Luke simply listed lands with large Jewish communities.

p: Gentiles who had converted to Judaism. Most Greek editions print these words at the start of 2:11.
b: A prosēlytos ("one who has come over") was a Gentile who had joined Israel fully: circumcision for men, immersion, and keeping the Law. They differ from "God-fearers," Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God without converting (10:2; 13:16). Nicolaus, one of the Seven, was "a proselyte from Antioch" (6:5). The words may describe only the visitors from Rome or the whole list; this translation sets them apart so that both readings stay open. The KJV prints them at the end of 2:10; modern Greek editions put them at the start of 2:11. This translation follows the KJV numbering used throughout the site.
orig: Ἰουδαῖοί τε καὶ προσήλυτοι (Ioudaioi te kai prosēlytoi)

a: about the great things of God
p: What the believers say in the many languages is praise: God's mighty acts.
b: Ta megaleia are "great deeds, wonders." The Greek Old Testament uses the word for what God did for Israel (Deuteronomy 11:2; Psalm 71:19), and Mary sings that "the Mighty One has worked great things for me" (Luke 1:49, a related word). So the tongues at Pentecost are not, as Luke tells it, preaching to the crowd, which comes with Peter's speech, but praise of God that strangers overhear. The same is said of the Gentiles at Caesarea, who are heard speaking in tongues and praising God (10:46).
orig: τὰ μεγαλεῖα τοῦ θεοῦ (ta megaleia tou theou)

p: Gleukos is sweet new wine. It is a sneer: the speakers sound drunk to those who cannot understand them.
b: Gleukos is sweet wine, new or kept sweet; at Pentecost, in early summer, the grape harvest was months away, so the word may simply mean strong sweet wine. The scoffers are probably those who heard only sounds they did not understand. Being filled with the Spirit and being drunk are set side by side again in Ephesians 5:18, and Hannah was once taken for drunk while praying (1 Samuel 1:13–15). Peter's reply (2:15) takes the charge at face value.
orig: γλεύκους μεμεστωμένοι (gleukous memestōmenoi)

a: Peter took his stand with the Eleven
p: The man who denied Jesus three times in a courtyard now speaks to thousands in the same city.
b: In Luke's Gospel Peter denied Jesus three times to servants and bystanders (Luke 22:54–62). Here he stands with the Eleven, the Twelve now complete again (1:26), and speaks to the crowd "freely" (2:29). Luke shows the change without comment. Jesus had prayed that Peter's faith would not fail, and told him to strengthen his brothers once he had turned back (Luke 22:31–32). The speech that follows is the first Christian sermon in Acts, and its pattern, Scripture, Jesus' death and resurrection, the apostles' witness, a call to repent, is repeated in later speeches.

a: the third hour of the day
p: Hours were counted from sunrise, about 6 a.m. The third hour is about 9 a.m.
b: Romans and Jews divided daylight into twelve hours, so the third hour is mid-morning, the time of the morning sacrifice and prayer in the temple. Drinking was an evening affair, so Peter's answer is a matter-of-fact one: no one is drunk at this hour. Later rabbinic custom held that on a feast day one did not eat or drink until after the morning prayers, but how early that custom is cannot be shown.

p: Peter quotes Joel's promise of the Spirit nearly word for word from the Greek Old Testament, with some changes.
b: Joel promised that after a time of locusts and repentance God would pour out his Spirit on all, with signs in the heavens before the day of the LORD (Joel 2:28–32; 3:1–5 in the Hebrew numbering). Peter's quotation follows the Greek Old Testament closely, but with changes that point to his meaning: "in the last days" instead of "after these things" (2:17), the young men's visions now placed before the old men's dreams (2:17), "and they will prophesy" added (2:18), and "above," "signs" and "below" added in 2:19, linking the cosmic "wonders and signs" to Jesus' "wonders and signs" in 2:22. "My" slaves in 2:18 is not a change: the Greek of Joel already has it, though the Hebrew does not (see the note there). Peter stops in the middle of Joel 2:32 and finishes the verse in his closing words (2:39).

p: Peter says the last days have begun. The Greek Old Testament of Joel reads "after these things."
b: Joel's Greek text, and Codex Vaticanus in Acts, say "after these things" (see the variant). Most witnesses to Acts read "in the last days," a phrase from Isaiah 2:2 and Micah 4:1, and that is almost certainly what Luke wrote: Peter is claiming that the end-time age foretold by the prophets has begun with Jesus and the Spirit. The New Testament speaks this way often (Hebrews 1:2; 1 Peter 1:20; 1 John 2:18). Christians differ on how long "the last days" last: the whole time between Jesus' first and second coming (the most common view), or a final period still ahead (many dispensationalists).
orig: ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις (en tais eschatais hēmerais)
r: Isaiah 2:2; Micah 4:1; Hebrews 1:2; 1 Peter 1:20; 2 Timothy 3:1; 1 John 2:18

p: A Hebrew way of saying all people. In Joel it means all Israel, young and old; Acts widens it in stages.
b: "All flesh" means all human beings (Isaiah 40:5, "all flesh will see it, all together"). In Joel the next words, "your sons and your daughters," show that the promise is to all Israel, without distinction of age, sex or rank. Acts follows that pattern step by step: first Jews from every nation (Acts 2), then Samaritans (8:17), then Gentiles (10:44–45), who receive the same gift "as we did."
orig: ἐπὶ πᾶσαν σάρκα (epi pasan sarka)

a: Your sons and your daughters will prophesy
p: Joel's promise names women. Acts later mentions Philip's four daughters who prophesied.
b: Women had been prophets in Israel (Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Anna in Luke 2:36), and Joel promises the Spirit to daughters and female slaves as to sons and male slaves. Acts mentions women praying with the apostles (1:14) and Philip's four unmarried daughters "who prophesied" (21:9), and Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in church (1 Corinthians 11:5). Christians who open preaching and leadership to women often begin with this verse; those who do not answer that prophesying, as Paul regulated it, is not the same as holding the office of teaching elder (1 Timothy 2:12). See the topic page.
r: Luke 2:36; 1:14; 21:9; 1 Corinthians 11:5; 1 Corinthians 14:34–35; 1 Timothy 2:12; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14

a: my slaves, both men and women
p: Douloi means "slaves." The Greek of Joel, which Acts follows, says "my slaves"; the Hebrew does not.
b: Doulos means a slave, a person owned by another, and this translation says "slave" where the Greek does (as in Jude 1:1), though many English Bibles soften it to "servant." Slavery in the Roman world was not based on race; slaves could be household managers or field hands, and many were freed. In Joel's Hebrew the promise reaches even the slaves of Israelite households, the lowest of all. The Greek of Joel and Acts says "my slaves," which makes them God's own servants, the way the believers call themselves God's slaves in 4:29.
orig: τοὺς δούλους μου καὶ ... τὰς δούλας μου (tous doulous mou kai ... tas doulas mou)

p: Peter adds "signs" to Joel's "wonders," making the phrase "wonders and signs" that he applies to Jesus next.
b: Joel has only "wonders in the heavens and on the earth." The words "above," "signs" and "below" are not in Joel; with them Peter makes the familiar pair "wonders and signs" from the exodus story (Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 6:22), which he uses of Jesus in 2:22 and which Acts uses of the apostles (2:43; 4:30; 5:12). Some readers connect the "blood and fire and haze of smoke" and the darkened sun (2:20) with the darkness at the crucifixion (Luke 23:44–45) and the fire of Pentecost; others take them as signs still to come before the end.

p: The Greek says the day of the Lord is "manifest, glorious." Joel's Hebrew says "dreadful."
b: Joel's Hebrew calls the day gadol venora', "great and dreadful." The Greek translators read nora' as if it came from the verb "to see" and wrote epiphanēs, "visible, splendid, shining," a word related to "epiphany." Acts follows the Greek. The Old Testament "day of the LORD" is the day God acts in judgment and rescue (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2:1–11; Malachi 4:5).
orig: ἡμέραν κυρίου τὴν μεγάλην καὶ ἐπιφανῆ (hēmeran kyriou tēn megalēn kai epiphanē)

t: Calling on the name of the Lord
p: In Joel "the Lord" is God's name, YHWH. Peter applies the promise to Jesus.
b: Joel 2:32 says "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD," using the divine name. The Greek has kyrios, "Lord," and Peter's speech goes on to show that God has made Jesus "Lord" (2:36) and to call people to be baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ" (2:38), since salvation is in no other name (4:12). Believers are soon known as those "who call on this name" (9:14, 21; 22:16), and Paul quotes Joel's line about Jesus (Romans 10:9–13). Scholars such as Larry Hurtado and Richard Bauckham see in this one of the earliest signs that Jesus was worshiped within Jewish monotheism.
orig: ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου (epikalesētai to onoma kyriou)

a: deeds of power, wonders and signs
p: Dynameis (powers), terata (wonders) and sēmeia (signs): what Jesus did, and what pointed beyond it.
b: A dynamis is a mighty act; a teras is a portent that makes people marvel; a sēmeion is a sign that points to a meaning. Peter says God did these "through" Jesus. Some readers find a low Christology here, Jesus as a man God worked through; others note that Peter speaks to Jews in terms they share and goes on to call Jesus Lord at God's right hand (2:33–36). "As you well know" is an appeal to public knowledge: the crowd had heard of Jesus' healings.
orig: δυνάμεσι καὶ τέρασι καὶ σημείοις (dynamesi kai terasi kai sēmeiois)

p: Peter holds both together: Jesus' death was God's set plan, and those who killed him are responsible.
b: Peter says Jesus was handed over "by the plan God had fixed and by what God knew ahead of time," and also that his hearers killed him. Acts says the same in the church's prayer (4:27–28). Reformed readers find here God's sovereign decree, which includes even sinful acts without making God their author (Westminster Confession 3.1). Arminian and Wesleyan readers stress foreknowledge and say God planned to use what he knew free people would do. Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks of God's eternal plan embracing human freedom (Catechism 599–600). All agree that the cross was not an accident or a defeat.
orig: τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ καὶ προγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ (tē hōrismenē boulē kai prognōsei tou theou)

a: the hands of men outside the law
p: Anomoi here means people without the Law of Moses, that is, Gentiles: the Roman soldiers.
b: Anomos can mean "lawless, wicked," but Jews also used it for Gentiles, who did not have the Torah (1 Corinthians 9:21, "to those outside the law"). The crucifixion was carried out by Roman soldiers under Pilate, and Luke's Gospel shows it (Luke 23:24–25, 33). So Peter distinguishes two parties: his Jerusalem hearers, who "handed him over" and asked for his death, and the Romans who "nailed him up." Translating "wicked men" hides the reference to the Romans.
orig: διὰ χειρὸς ἀνόμων (dia cheiros anomōn)

a: to nail him up and kill him
p: Peter accuses the Jerusalem crowd of his own day. Later Christians wrongly turned such words against all Jews.
b: Peter, a Jew, speaks to fellow Jews in Jerusalem weeks after the crucifixion, some of whom may have been in the crowd before Pilate (Luke 23:13–25). He blames them as a prophet would, in order to call them to repent, and he says they acted "without understanding" (3:17); three thousand respond. Later, when the church was mostly Gentile, such verses were read as a charge against the Jewish people of every age, the "deicide" accusation that fed centuries of persecution. The Catholic Church at the Second Vatican Council rejected that reading: the death of Christ "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today" (Nostra Aetate 4), and most Protestant and Orthodox churches agree.

a: untying the birth pains of death
p: A mixed picture from the Greek Psalms: death's "cords" in Hebrew became death's "birth pains."
b: In Psalm 18:4–5 and 116:3, the Hebrew chevlei mavet means "death's ropes": "Death's ropes closed around me" (Psalm 116:3). But chevel can also mean "labor pain," and the Greek translators wrote ōdines, "birth pangs." Peter's words keep both pictures: God "untied" (as one loosens ropes) the "birth pains" of death. The church fathers saw a meaning in it: death, like a woman in labor, could not hold the one it carried, and had to give him up to new life.
orig: λύσας τὰς ὠδῖνας τοῦ θανάτου (lysas tas ōdinas tou thanatou)

t: Psalm 16: David speaking of himself, or of the Messiah?
p: Peter argues that Psalm 16 cannot be about David himself, since David died and his tomb is still there.
b: Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust: "you will not allow your loyal one to see the Pit" (Psalm 16:10). Read in its own setting, it is David's prayer that God will keep him alive and safe, and Jewish interpreters read it that way. Peter's argument (2:29–31) is that David died and decayed, so the words were not fully true of him; as a prophet he was speaking of his descendant the Messiah, who did not see decay. The Greek translation helps the argument: where the Hebrew has "the Pit," the Greek has "decay" (diaphthora), and "safety" becomes "hope." Paul uses the same argument at Pisidian Antioch (13:35–37).

a: Even my flesh will make its home in hope
p: The Greek Psalm says "in hope"; the Hebrew says "in safety." The verb means "to pitch a tent."
b: The site's Psalm 16:9 reads "even my flesh will settle down in safety," from the Hebrew lavetach, "securely." The Greek translation, which Peter follows, says ep' elpidi, "in hope," which suits Peter's point that David's body rested in hope of resurrection. The verb kataskēnoō means "to camp, to dwell in a tent," an image of the body at rest. "My tongue celebrated" also follows the Greek; the Hebrew has "my glory" or "my honor."
orig: ἡ σάρξ μου κατασκηνώσει ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι (hē sarx mou kataskēnōsei ep' elpidi)

a: you will not allow your holy one to see decay
p: The Hebrew has hasid, "loyal one," and shachat, "pit." The Greek says "holy one" and "decay."
b: The Hebrew chasid is one who keeps loyal love (hesed), so the site's Psalm says "your loyal one"; the Greek translators chose hosios, "holy, devout," which became a title of Jesus (13:35). The Hebrew shachat means "pit, grave," though a similar word means "ruin"; the Greek diaphthora means "decay, corruption." The KJV's "thy Holy One to see corruption" follows the Greek. Many Christians also read "you will not leave my life behind in Hades" as speaking of Christ's descent to the dead (1 Peter 3:19; 4:6); see the card at Psalm 16.
orig: τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν διαφθοράν (ton hosion sou idein diaphthoran)

a: his tomb is among us still today
p: David was buried in the City of David. Josephus says the tomb was still known, and robbed, in his time.
b: "David lay down with his ancestors, and they buried him in the City of David" (1 Kings 2:10), and Nehemiah 3:16 mentions "David's tombs" in Jerusalem. Josephus says the high priest John Hyrcanus took silver from David's tomb, and that Herod later tried to rob it too (Jewish Antiquities 7.392–394; 16.179–183). So Peter could point to it: everyone knew where David lay. The building on Mount Zion now called the Tomb of David dates from the Middle Ages and is not the ancient site.

p: The Bible never calls David a prophet in so many words, but Jews of the time did.
b: David speaks by the Spirit in 2 Samuel 23:2: "The LORD's Spirit has spoken by me." The Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a, column 27) says David composed thousands of psalms and songs and "all these he spoke through prophecy given him from before the Most High." Josephus also calls David a prophet. Peter's reasoning follows: as a prophet who knew God's oath to him, David looked ahead to his descendant. The oath is Psalm 132:11, "From the fruit of your body I will set one on your throne," based on 2 Samuel 7:12–16.

a: raised high at God's right hand
p: The Greek dative can mean "exalted to God's right hand" or "exalted by God's right hand," his power.
b: Tē dexia tou theou may mean place, at or to God's right hand, as Psalm 110:1 in 2:34 suggests, or means, "by God's right hand," as in Psalm 118:16, "The right hand of the LORD lifts high." Both are true in Peter's argument, and he may mean both. The "right hand" is the seat of honor and power beside a king. Jesus receives the promised Spirit and pours it out: the gift that only God could give (Joel 2:28) now comes from Jesus.
orig: τῇ δεξιᾷ οὖν τοῦ θεοῦ ὑψωθείς (tē dexia oun tou theou hypsōtheis)

a: David did not go up into the heavens
p: The Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often. Jesus himself used it about the Messiah.
b: "The LORD declares to my lord: 'Sit at my right hand'" (Psalm 110:1) is quoted or echoed more than twenty times in the New Testament (Mark 12:36; Matthew 22:44; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Hebrews 1:13). Jesus used it to ask how the Messiah could be David's son and David's Lord (Luke 20:41–44). Peter's argument is short: David did not ascend, so "my Lord" is someone other than David; Jesus has ascended, so it is he. In its own setting the psalm addresses a king of David's line, and the Greek's "The Lord said to my Lord" hides the difference in the Hebrew between YHWH and adoni, "my lord." Some Jewish interpreters read "my lord" as Abraham (so the Talmud, Nedarim 32b) or as David himself.
r: Psalm 110:1; Luke 20:41–44; Matthew 22:41–46; Mark 12:35–37; Hebrews 1:13; 1 Corinthians 15:25

a: God has made him both Lord and Messiah
p: Did Jesus become Lord at his resurrection? Some read an early "adoptionist" view here; most read a public enthronement.
b: Adoptionist or exaltation reading: some scholars (for example James Dunn) see here a very early belief that Jesus was made Lord and Messiah when God raised him, before the church spoke of his divine status from birth or before creation. Later "adoptionists" taught that Jesus was a man adopted as God's Son. Common reading: Luke himself calls Jesus "Messiah and Lord" at his birth (Luke 2:11), so "made" means God has installed and shown him as what he already was, as a crown prince is enthroned (compare Romans 1:4, "declared Son of God with power"). Either way, "Lord" here sets Jesus in the place of the "my Lord" of Psalm 110:1.
orig: καὶ κύριον αὐτὸν καὶ χριστὸν ἐποίησεν ὁ θεός (kai kyrion auton kai christon epoiēsen ho theos)

p: Greek christos translates Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one." As a title it is "the Messiah"; in a name, "Christ."
b: Kings and priests in Israel were anointed with oil, and "the LORD's anointed" was a title of the king (1 Samuel 24:6; Psalm 2:2). By Jesus' time many Jews hoped for an anointed king of David's line. This translation writes "the Messiah" where Acts uses christos as a title (2:31, 36; 3:18, 20; 4:26), so that readers can see the claim being made, and "Christ" where it has become part of Jesus' name ("Jesus Christ," 2:38; 3:6; 4:10). The followers of this Messiah were first called "Christians" at Antioch (11:26).
orig: χριστόν (christon)

p: Metanoeō: to change one's mind and direction, to turn from sin to God.
b: Metanoia literally means "change of mind," but in the Bible it carries the Hebrew idea of turning back (shuv), a change of life, not just regret. Peter pairs it with "turn around" in 3:19. John the Baptist and Jesus both preached repentance (Luke 3:3; 5:32; 24:47), and Jesus said repentance for the forgiveness of sins would be preached in his name to all nations beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). This is where that begins.
orig: Μετανοήσατε (Metanoēsate)

a: be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ
p: Acts speaks of baptism "in the name of Jesus," Matthew of baptism into the threefold name. How do they fit?
b: The Greek here is epi tō onomati, "on the name" (Vaticanus and Bezae read en, "in"); elsewhere Acts says "in" or "into" the name of the Lord Jesus (8:16; 10:48; 19:5). Matthew 28:19 has "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Most churches read Acts as describing what kind of baptism it was, Christian baptism, calling on Jesus and placing the person under his authority, not as giving the words to be spoken, and they baptize with the threefold name, as the Didache 7 already did. Oneness Pentecostals hold that the name of the Father, Son and Spirit is Jesus, and that Acts 2:38 gives the required formula. See the card at Matthew 28:19.
orig: βαπτισθήτω ἕκαστος ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (baptisthētō hekastos hymōn epi tō onomati Iēsou Christou)

a: for the forgiveness of your sins
p: The Greek eis usually means "toward, for the purpose of." Some argue it can mean "because of."
b: Eis aphesin hamartiōn is the phrase used of John's baptism (Luke 3:3; Mark 1:4) and of Jesus' blood, "poured out for many, so that sins can be forgiven" (Matthew 26:28), as the site renders it there. Most grammarians take eis as "with a view to, in order to obtain." Some Baptist scholars, following Julius Mantey, argued for a causal sense, "because of" forgiveness already received; Ralph Marcus answered in the same journal (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1951–52) that the causal sense is not proven in this kind of phrase. Many who read "in order to" still say forgiveness comes through the repentance and faith that baptism expresses (10:43). The traditions differ on this; see the card on the chapter page.
orig: εἰς ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ὑμῶν (eis aphesin tōn hamartiōn hymōn)

p: Echoes Isaiah 57:19 and Joel 2:32. Peter may mean distant Jews; Luke's readers would think of Gentiles too.
b: Isaiah promised "'Peace, peace, to the one who is far and the one who is near'" (Isaiah 57:19), and the rest of Joel 2:32 speaks of survivors "whom the LORD calls"; Peter ends with that phrase, "all whom the Lord our God calls." On Peter's lips at this point "those far away" may mean Jews scattered in distant lands and future generations, since he will learn about Gentiles only in Acts 10. But Luke's readers would hear more: Ephesians 2:13–17 uses the same Isaiah verse of Gentiles brought near, and in 22:21 the Lord sends Paul far away to the Gentiles.

p: Moses' words for Israel in the wilderness, used by Jesus too. Peter calls for rescue from a generation under judgment.
b: In the Song of Moses, Israel is "a warped and twisted generation" (Deuteronomy 32:5), and Psalm 78:8 speaks of "a generation that was stubborn and defiant." Jesus used similar words of his own generation (Luke 9:41; 11:29–32). "Be saved" is passive in Greek: God does the rescuing, and the hearers are to let it happen by repenting and being baptized. Paul uses the same phrase of the world his readers live in (Philippians 2:15).
orig: ἀπὸ τῆς γενεᾶς τῆς σκολιᾶς ταύτης (apo tēs geneas tēs skolias tautēs)

p: A large number some historians doubt. Many readers set it beside Sinai, where three thousand died.
b: Historical questions: could three thousand be baptized in a day in Jerusalem? Supporters point to the many ritual immersion pools (mikvaot) found near the temple's southern steps, and to the pools of Siloam and Bethesda; skeptics such as Ernst Haenchen took the numbers in Acts (2:41; 4:4) as Luke's way of showing growth. Typology: after the golden calf, at the time of the giving of the Law, "About three thousand of the people fell that day" (Exodus 32:28). Many readers contrast the two: the Law brought death to three thousand, the Spirit life to three thousand (compare 2 Corinthians 3:6). This contrast is an interpretation, not stated by Luke.

p: Koinōnia: partnership, a shared life. It includes sharing possessions (2:44–45).
b: Koinōnia comes from koinos, "common," the word in 2:44 ("in common"). It means sharing in something with others: a business partnership, a gift for the poor (Romans 15:26; 2 Corinthians 8:4), or fellowship with God and one another (1 John 1:3). With the article, "the fellowship" may mean the community itself, or its shared meals, or its common fund. Luke's four marks of the church, teaching, fellowship, the bread and the prayers, are often read as a pattern for church life.
orig: τῇ κοινωνίᾳ (tē koinōnia)

p: The Lord's Supper, or the community's ordinary meals, or both together.
b: Jewish meals began with the head of the house breaking bread with a blessing, so "breaking bread" can mean simply eating together (27:35). But Luke uses the phrase with weight: the risen Jesus was known to the two at Emmaus "in the breaking of the bread" (Luke 24:30, 35), and at Troas the church gathers on the first day of the week "to break bread" (20:7). Most interpreters think the early church ate the Lord's Supper as part of a shared meal (1 Corinthians 11:20–26), so 2:42 and 2:46 describe both. Catholic and Orthodox readers see the Eucharist here; some Protestant readers see ordinary fellowship meals.
orig: τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου (tē klasei tou artou)

p: With the article, probably set prayers: the temple's hours of prayer and Jewish forms the believers kept.
b: Luke writes "the prayers," plural, with the article. The believers went daily to the temple (2:46), and Peter and John go up "for the hour of prayer" (3:1). They likely kept the Jewish times of prayer and used familiar prayers, adding prayers in Jesus' name, such as the Lord's Prayer, which the Didache (8:2–3) says to pray three times a day. The church's later fixed hours of prayer (the daily office) look back to this verse.

p: A Greek ideal, a Jewish promise and a practice at Qumran. Was it a rule for the church, or a moment?
b: Greeks said "friends hold all things in common" (Aristotle quotes the proverb in Nicomachean Ethics 9.8), and Luke's words would remind educated readers of it. Moses had said "there will be no one in need among you" (Deuteronomy 15:4), and 4:34 echoes that verse. The community of the Dead Sea Scrolls required members to hand over their property to the group (Community Rule, 1QS 6:19–22). In Acts it is voluntary: Peter tells Ananias that his property was his own to keep (5:4), and people still have houses (12:12). Readings: a model for all Christians, for some (monasteries, the Hutterites), an ideal of generous sharing, or an early experiment. See the card on chapter 4.
orig: εἶχον ἅπαντα κοινά (eichon hapanta koina)

a: Day after day they kept going to the temple
p: The first believers were Jews who kept worshiping at the temple. Acts does not show them leaving Judaism.
b: Luke's Gospel ends with the disciples "in the Temple all the time, blessing God" (Luke 24:53), and Acts begins the same way: the believers meet in the temple courts, Peter and John go up at the hour of prayer (3:1), and they gather in Solomon's Porch (5:12). Paul too worships in the temple years later (21:26; 24:11–12). For Luke the movement is the true continuation of Israel, "the Way" within the Jewish people, not a new religion. Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen and Alan Segal also describe the first believers as a Jewish messianic group.

a: In one house after another they broke bread
p: The believers met in homes. For their first two centuries Christians met mostly in houses, not church buildings.
b: Kat' oikon means "house by house" or "at home." Early Christian worship and meals took place in private houses large enough for a group: Mary's house in Jerusalem (12:12), Lydia's at Philippi (16:15, 40), Priscilla and Aquila's (1 Corinthians 16:19; Romans 16:5). The oldest known house adapted as a church, at Dura-Europos in Syria, dates from about AD 240, and by the late 200s some cities had larger church buildings, such as the one at Nicomedia destroyed in 303. The household, with its slaves and dependents, shaped early church life.
orig: κλῶντές τε κατ᾽ οἶκον ἄρτον (klōntes te kat' oikon arton)

p: A present passive: salvation as God's ongoing work, one person after another.
b: Tous sōzomenous is present tense and passive: "those who were being saved." The Lord (Jesus, or God) is the one who saves and adds. Paul uses the same participle for believers (1 Corinthians 1:18; 2 Corinthians 2:15). Some readers find here salvation as a process begun and not yet finished; others simply "those who were saved" day by day, as the KJV renders it, "such as should be saved," a phrase sometimes read as predestination.
orig: τοὺς σῳζομένους (tous sōzomenous)

a: the hour of prayer, the ninth hour of the day
p: About 3 p.m., the time of the afternoon sacrifice in the temple, when crowds gathered to pray.
b: Two lambs were offered in the temple each day, one in the morning and one "between the evenings" (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8). By the first century the afternoon offering was made about the ninth hour, 3 p.m., and people gathered in the courts to pray while incense was offered (Luke 1:10; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 14.65; Mishnah, tractate Tamid). Daniel prayed "at the time of the evening offering" (Daniel 9:21), and Cornelius prays at the same hour (10:3, 30). Peter and John keep the Jewish hours of prayer.

p: No doctor could explain this healing away. Paul heals a man described with the same words at Lystra.
b: The man had never walked (4:22 says he was over forty), so the healing could not be a slow recovery or a trick; everyone in the temple knew him (3:10). Luke tells a matching story about Paul at Lystra, where a man "lame from his mother's womb" who had never walked jumps up and walks (14:8–10), one of many parallels between Peter in the first half of Acts and Paul in the second. Jesus' own healings of the lame (Luke 5:17–26; 7:22) are signs that the time Isaiah promised has come.

p: No other ancient source names a "Beautiful Gate." It may be the bronze Nicanor Gate, or a gate on the east.
b: Josephus describes the temple's gates in detail but never calls one "Beautiful." Most scholars think Luke means the great gate of Corinthian bronze that Josephus says far outshone the others in value (Jewish War 5.201), probably the one the Mishnah calls the Nicanor Gate (Middot 1:4; 2:3), between the Court of the Gentiles or Court of the Women and the inner courts. Others suggest the Shushan Gate on the east wall facing the Mount of Olives. A beggar would sit where worshipers passed on their way to prayer and were most mindful of almsgiving.

t: Alms, and the lame at the temple
p: Giving to the poor was a religious duty, so the temple gate was a good place to beg. But the lame man stayed outside.
b: Eleēmosynē, "alms," is from the word for mercy; Jews counted giving to the poor among the chief acts of devotion (Tobit 4:7–11; Luke 11:41). The man sits at the gate, not inside. The law kept priests with a disability from offering sacrifices ("no man who is blind or lame," Leviticus 21:18), and a saying from David's time ran "No one blind or lame may come into the house" (2 Samuel 5:8); the Dead Sea community barred the lame from its assembly (1QSa 2:3–9). How strictly the temple courts were closed to the lame is not known, but the healed man goes in with Peter and John, walking and leaping and praising God (3:8).
orig: ἐλεημοσύνην (eleēmosynēn)

a: I own no silver and no gold
p: A line the church has quoted against itself. A famous story is told of Thomas Aquinas and a pope.
b: Peter and John have nothing to give but Jesus' name, and the believers' goods were held in common (2:44–45). A story told since the late Middle Ages has Thomas Aquinas visiting the pope while money was being counted; the pope said the church could no longer say "silver and gold I have none," and Thomas answered that neither could it say "rise and walk." The story is probably legend, but it shows how this verse became a measure for the church's wealth and power.
orig: Ἀργύριον καὶ χρυσίον οὐχ ὑπάρχει μοι (Argyrion kai chrysion ouch hyparchei moi)

a: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene
p: The name stands for the person and his authority. Healing in Jesus' name is not a spell.
b: In the Bible a name stands for the person: to act in someone's name is to act with his authority, as his representative. "The name" of Jesus is a leading theme of chapters 3–4 (3:16; 4:7, 10, 12, 17–18, 30). Acts makes clear it is not a magic formula: when the sons of Sceva try to use "the name of the Jesus whom Paul preaches" as a spell, the evil spirit turns on them (19:13–16). The healing comes from the risen Jesus himself, through faith (3:16; 9:34).
orig: ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Ναζωραίου (en tō onomati Iēsou Christou tou Nazōraiou)

a: the soles of his feet and his ankles
p: Precise words like these led some to argue for a physician's vocabulary. Henry Cadbury showed others used them too.
b: Paul calls Luke "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14). In 1882 William Hobart listed hundreds of words in Luke-Acts, such as basis, "sole" or "foot," and sphydron, "ankle," that also occur in Greek medical writers, and argued that the author was a doctor. In 1920 Henry Cadbury showed that most of these words were used just as often by educated writers who were not doctors, such as Josephus and Lucian. Most scholars now say the vocabulary fits a doctor but does not prove one; the case for Luke rests on the tradition and on the "we" passages.
orig: αἱ βάσεις αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ σφυδρά (hai baseis autou kai ta sphydra)

a: With a leap he was on his feet
p: Isaiah promised that in the age of salvation the lame would leap like a deer.
b: Isaiah 35 pictures God's people coming home through a desert in bloom: "Then a lame man will jump like a deer, / and a mute tongue will sing out" (Isaiah 35:6). The Greek of Isaiah uses hallomai, "to leap" (haleitai, "will leap"), the verb Luke uses here ("leaping," 3:8) and in 14:10. Jesus pointed to such healings as signs of his mission (Luke 7:22). The man's leaping, walking and praising in the temple is the prophecy acted out.
orig: ἐξαλλόμενος ἔστη (exallomenos estē)

p: A covered colonnade on the east side of the temple's outer court, where Jesus had walked and taught.
b: Josephus describes the porches that lined the great outer court, and says the eastern one was believed to go back to Solomon (Jewish Antiquities 20.220–221; Jewish War 5.185). Jesus walked there at the Feast of Dedication: "Jesus was walking around in the temple, in Solomon's Porch" (John 10:23). The believers made it their meeting place (5:12), in full public view, in the court open to everyone, Jews and Gentiles.
orig: τῇ στοᾷ τῇ καλουμένῃ Σολομῶντος (tē stoa tē kaloumenē Solomōntos)

a: as if we had made him walk through some power or holiness of our own
p: Peter turns attention from himself to Jesus. Acts repeats the point when people try to honor apostles as gods.
b: Eusebeia, "godliness, piety," was a prized virtue in the Greek world. Peter denies that the healing came from his own spiritual power or piety, the kind of claim made for wonder-workers of the time. The same refusal returns when Cornelius bows to Peter (10:25–26) and when the crowd at Lystra calls Paul and Barnabas gods (14:14–15). In contrast, Simon the sorcerer claims to be "someone great" (8:9) and Herod accepts divine honors and dies (12:22–23).
orig: ἰδίᾳ δυνάμει ἢ εὐσεβείᾳ (idia dynamei ē eusebeia)

a: the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob
p: Peter names God as he named himself to Moses at the burning bush.
b: At the bush God told Moses to say: "The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you" (Exodus 3:15). Jesus quoted this name to show that God is God of the living (Luke 20:37–38). Peter uses it to insist that the God who raised Jesus is Israel's own God, not a new one. Jewish prayer still opens the same way, in the first blessing of the Amidah, the daily standing prayer: "God of Abraham, God of Isaac and God of Jacob."

p: Pais means "servant" or "child." The phrase recalls Isaiah's servant who would be "glorified." The KJV says "his Son."
b: Pais can mean "child" or "servant." Acts uses it of Jesus only in early prayers and speeches (3:13, 26; 4:27, 30) and of David (4:25), so most translators read "servant." Isaiah's servant song opens with the same words in the Greek: "my servant ... will be lifted up and glorified" (Isaiah 52:13, Greek). The site's Hebrew-based rendering is "Look, my servant will succeed" (Isaiah 52:13). Peter's "has given glory to his servant" points to that song, which goes on to the servant's suffering (Isaiah 53). The KJV's "his Son Jesus" is a possible meaning of the word but hides the link to Isaiah.
orig: ἐδόξασεν τὸν παῖδα αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦν (edoxasen ton paida autou Iēsoun)

p: Two titles: "the Holy One" and "the Righteous One." The second is used of Jesus three times in Acts.
b: Demons call Jesus "the Holy One of God" in Luke 4:34; Peter in 2:27 called him God's "holy one" from Psalm 16. "The Righteous One" is a title Stephen and Ananias use for Jesus (7:52; 22:14), echoing Isaiah's "the righteous one, my servant" (Isaiah 53:11) and the centurion's words at the cross that Jesus was righteous (Luke 23:47). The irony is sharp: the crowd disowned the righteous one and asked for a murderer, Barabbas, who had been jailed for rebellion and murder (Luke 23:18–25).

p: Archēgos: leader, founder, pioneer, prince. The KJV says "Prince of life."
b: An archēgos was the founder of a city or family, the leader who goes first, or a prince. The word is used of Jesus again in 5:31 ("Leader and Savior") and in Hebrews 2:10 and 12:2 (the "pioneer" of salvation and of faith). Here the paradox is the point: they killed the very one who is the source and leader of life, and asked for the release of one who took life. Readers differ on whether Peter means "the author of life" (the source of all life, as in John 1:4) or "the leader into life" (the first to rise, who leads others to resurrection).
orig: τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς ζωῆς (ton archēgon tēs zōēs)

a: It was on the basis of faith in his name
p: The Greek of this verse is awkward, and some think it shows an Aramaic source behind Peter's speech.
b: Literally: "And on the faith of his name, this man whom you see and know his name made strong, and the faith which is through him gave him this soundness." The repetitions of "his name" and "faith" are hard to put into smooth Greek or English. Charles Torrey argued that Luke translated an Aramaic document for Acts 1–15 and that this verse shows a misread Aramaic phrase; most scholars think Luke wrote the speeches himself in a Greek with deliberate Old Testament color. Either way the sense is clear: the power is Jesus' name, received by faith, and even that faith comes "through him."
orig: ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ (epi tē pistei tou onomatos autou)

a: you did not understand what you were doing
p: Peter softens his charge: the people and their rulers did not understand. Luke's Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them."
b: The Greek is kata agnoian, "in ignorance." The Law distinguished sins done unknowingly, for which atonement could be made, from defiant sins (Numbers 15:27–31). Peter places his hearers' guilt in the first group and invites them to repent. In Luke's Gospel Jesus prays from the cross for forgiveness for those who "do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34; the verse is missing from some early manuscripts). Paul speaks the same way of the rulers of this age (1 Corinthians 2:8) and of his own past (1 Timothy 1:13). The verse stands against the later Christian claim that the Jewish people knowingly killed God.
orig: κατὰ ἄγνοιαν ἐπράξατε (kata agnoian epraxate)

p: Peter says all the prophets foretold the Messiah's suffering. Where? And did Jews of the time expect it?
b: Jesus told the disciples on the Emmaus road that the Messiah "had to" suffer according to Moses and all the prophets (Luke 24:25–27, 44–46). The New Testament points chiefly to Isaiah 52:13–53:12 and to the Psalms of the suffering righteous one (Psalm 22; 69). Most Jewish hopes of the time pictured a victorious king, and Jewish readers have usually taken Isaiah 53 to describe Israel, or a prophet, rather than the Messiah. Some later rabbinic texts do speak of a Messiah who suffers or dies, such as the Messiah son of Joseph (Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 52a), though how early that idea is remains debated. For Peter, the suffering itself proves that God's plan was carried out.

p: Anapsyxis is a cool breath, rest after strain. Peter links Israel's repentance with the coming of God's renewal.
b: Anapsyxis means a cooling, a chance to catch one's breath. The "times of relief" come "from the Lord's presence" (literally "from the face of the Lord"), and with them God's sending of the Messiah (3:20). Many readers think Peter means the final renewal at Jesus' return, which Israel's repentance would help bring; a similar idea appears in rabbinic sayings that Israel's repentance would bring redemption (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b). Others think the times of relief are the present blessings of forgiveness and the Spirit. In the KJV this clause ends 3:19; modern Greek editions print it at the start of 3:20.
orig: καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως (kairoi anapsyxeōs)

p: Most read it as the renewal the prophets promised. Origen and Gregory of Nyssa hoped all would be saved.
b: Apokatastasis comes from the verb of 1:6, "restore the kingdom to Israel," and of Malachi's promise in the Greek that Elijah would "restore" hearts (Malachi 4:6); Jesus said Elijah would "set everything right again" (Matthew 17:11). Common reading: the renewal of Israel and creation that the prophets foretold, "of which God spoke" through them, at Jesus' return (Isaiah 65:17; Romans 8:19–21). Universalist reading: Origen and Gregory of Nyssa used the word for the final return of all creatures, even the wicked and perhaps the devil, to God. Anathemas against Origen's teaching were attached to the Council of Constantinople in 553, and most churches reject universal salvation; see the card on the chapter page.
orig: ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων (apokatastaseōs pantōn)
r: 1:6; Malachi 4:6; Matthew 17:11; Isaiah 65:17; Romans 8:19–21; 1 Corinthians 15:28; Colossians 1:20

p: Jesus' time in heaven is part of God's plan too: the same word dei, "it is necessary."
b: Peter uses Luke's word of divine necessity again (see 1:16): it is God's plan that heaven receive Jesus until the restoration. This gives the church's present age its shape: Jesus is absent in body, reigning at God's right hand (2:33), and active through the Spirit and his name (3:16), until he is sent again (3:20). Lutheran and Reformed theologians argued over this verse in the 1500s: the Reformed saw it as showing that Christ's body is in heaven, not present in the Supper; Lutherans answered that God's right hand is everywhere.
orig: ὃν δεῖ οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι (hon dei ouranon men dexasthai)

p: Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him. Peter says the promise points to Jesus.
b: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers. You must listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15).
