In its own setting the promise may mean a line of prophets after Moses, and Jewish interpreters have read it so; but by Jesus' time some expected one great prophet: the Dead Sea community quoted it in a list of messianic texts (4QTestimonia), the Samaritans looked for a prophet-like-Moses called the Taheb, and people asked whether John or Jesus was "the Prophet" (John 1:21; 6:14). Stephen quotes the same verse (7:37). At the transfiguration the voice said of Jesus, "Listen to him" (Luke 9:35), the words of Deuteronomy 18:15.

a: will be wiped out from among the people
p: The warning blends Deuteronomy 18:19 with the penalty of Leviticus 23:29 for not keeping the Day of Atonement.
b: Deuteronomy 18:19 says God will "call to account" anyone who will not listen to the prophet. Peter's words instead use the strong phrase of Leviticus 23:29: "Any person who does not humble himself on that very day will be cut off from his kin." The Greek of Leviticus has "will be utterly destroyed from his people," the words Peter uses. Joining verses that share a word was a normal Jewish way of reading Scripture. The warning is sharp, but it is spoken to call Israel to listen, not to cut Israel off: the next verses call them heirs of the covenant (3:25).
orig: ἐξολεθρευθήσεται ἐκ τοῦ λαοῦ (exolethreuthēsetai ek tou laou)

a: Samuel and those who followed him one after another
p: Samuel was counted the first of the prophets after Moses. He anointed David, the king of the promise.
b: Jewish tradition counted Samuel as the first in the line of prophets after Moses (1 Samuel 3:20 calls him a prophet recognized by all Israel), and Paul's speech also moves from the judges to "Samuel the prophet" (13:20). Samuel anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13), and Nathan's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16) is the root of Peter's argument in 2:30. "These days" are the days of the Messiah and the Spirit.

a: In your offspring all the clans of the earth will be blessed
p: Peter quotes God's promise to Abraham, blending Genesis 22:18 and 12:3. The blessing is for all peoples.
b: God promised Abraham, "All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you" (Genesis 12:3), and after the binding of Isaac, "all the nations of the earth will bless themselves by your offspring" (Genesis 22:18). Peter's words mix the two ("clans," "offspring"). The Hebrew verb can be read as "be blessed" or "bless themselves"; the Greek, which Peter follows, says "be blessed." "Offspring" (literally "seed") can mean Abraham's descendants or one descendant; Paul reads it of Christ (Galatians 3:16), and Peter in 3:26 may mean the same.
orig: ἐν τῷ σπέρματί σου (en tō spermati sou)
r: Genesis 12:3; Genesis 18:18; Genesis 22:18; Genesis 26:4; Galatians 3:8; Galatians 3:16

p: Israel hears first; the nations follow. The order runs through Acts and Paul's letters.
b: Peter tells his Jewish hearers that they are the first to receive God's servant and his blessing; the word "first" implies others will follow, the "clans of the earth" of 3:25. Paul follows this order in every city, synagogue first (13:46; 17:2), and writes "to the Jew first and also to the Greek" (Romans 1:16). Readers debate whether "raised up" here means God sent Jesus as the prophet he "raised up" (3:22) or raised him from the dead (3:15); the same Greek verb serves both.
orig: ὑμῖν πρῶτον (hymin prōton)

a: as each of you turns away from your evil deeds
p: The Greek can mean "by turning each of you away" (God's act) or "as each of you turns away" (the hearers' act).
b: En tō apostrephein can be transitive, "by turning you away from your wickedness," so that the blessing is the turning God works in people, or intransitive, "in your turning away," so that the blessing comes as they turn. Both fit Luke's theology: God gives repentance (5:31; 11:18), and people are called to repent (3:19). Many translations choose the first; this one the second, to match the call of 3:19.
orig: ἐν τῷ ἀποστρέφειν ἕκαστον (en tō apostrephein hekaston)

p: The priest in charge of the temple police, second only to the high priest.
b: The stratēgos tou hierou was the officer who kept order in the temple with a force of Levite guards; Josephus mentions him (Jewish War 6.294; Jewish Antiquities 20.131), and later Jewish sources call the office segan, the high priest's deputy. Jesus was arrested by such officers (Luke 22:4, 52). The temple authorities act because the apostles are drawing crowds and teaching in the temple courts without their permission.
orig: ὁ στρατηγὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ (ho stratēgos tou hierou)

p: The party of the priestly aristocracy. They denied the resurrection, which is why the apostles' preaching angered them.
b: The Sadducees were a party drawn from the leading priestly families and the wealthy; the high priest belonged to them (5:17). Josephus says they denied life after death and rewards and punishments beyond this life, and accepted only what was written (Jewish Antiquities 18.16; Jewish War 2.164–165). Luke notes that they say there is no resurrection, nor angel nor spirit (23:8; Luke 20:27). The Pharisees, by contrast, believed in the resurrection, and in Acts they are sometimes the apostles' defenders (5:34–39; 23:6–9). The Sadducees vanished as a party after the temple fell in AD 70.

a: in Jesus there is resurrection from the dead
p: Either "in the case of Jesus" (his resurrection proves the dead will rise) or "through Jesus" (he brings it).
b: En tō Iēsou can mean "in the person of Jesus," pointing to his own rising as the example and proof of the resurrection of the dead, or "by means of Jesus," the one through whom the dead will be raised. Paul holds both: Christ is "the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). For the Sadducees, who denied any resurrection, the apostles' claim was offensive on two counts: it taught a doctrine they rejected, and it named as God's agent a man the priests had handed over to Rome.
orig: ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ τὴν ἀνάστασιν τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν (en tō Iēsou tēn anastasin tēn ek nekrōn)

p: The Greek says "men," andres. Luke's numbers show rapid growth; historians debate how exact they are.
b: Luke usually uses anēr for males, so the count may be of men alone, as in the feeding of the five thousand (Luke 9:14); or it may mean people in general, and the total of believers so far. Jerusalem's population in the first century is estimated very differently, from about 25,000 to more than 80,000, so the figure would be a large share of the city. Some historians take Luke's numbers as round estimates or literary signs of the word's success (2:41; 6:7; 21:20); others note that Luke elsewhere is careful with details and see no reason to doubt that the movement grew fast.
orig: ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῶν ἀνδρῶν ὡς χιλιάδες πέντε (ho arithmos tōn andrōn hōs chiliades pente)

a: their rulers, the elders and the scribes
p: The same body that tried Jesus: chief priests, elders from leading families, and experts in the Law.
b: The Sanhedrin (4:15) was Jerusalem's high council under the high priest. Luke names its three groups as he did at Jesus' trial (Luke 22:66): the "rulers," here the chief priests; the "elders," heads of leading lay families; and the "scribes," experts in the law of Moses, many of them Pharisees. The Mishnah, compiled later, says the great Sanhedrin had seventy-one members (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6), but how it worked in the first century is debated. Under Roman rule it governed Jewish affairs in Judea but could not, according to John 18:31, carry out the death penalty.

p: Annas was high priest AD 6–15; his son-in-law Caiaphas, AD 18–36. Caiaphas' family tomb may have been found.
b: Rome appointed and removed high priests. Annas (Ananus son of Seth) held the office from AD 6 to 15, and five of his sons later did too, so he remained the power in the family and was still called "high priest" (Luke 3:2; John 18:13). Caiaphas, his son-in-law (John 18:13), was high priest from about AD 18 to 36. In 1990 a burial cave in Jerusalem yielded an ornate bone box inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas"; Josephus gives Caiaphas' name as Joseph, and many scholars identify the box as his, though some doubt it. "John" may be Jonathan son of Annas, high priest in AD 36–37 (see the variant); "Alexander" is unknown.

p: The council asks about power and name: who authorized this, or what force did you call on?
b: In the ancient world healers and exorcists called on the names of gods, angels or famous figures, and Jewish law punished those who led Israel astray with signs done in another god's name (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). The question is a formal one in a hearing: by whose authority do you act? It gives Peter the opening for his answer: "the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene" (4:10), and his claim that there is no other saving name (4:12). The emphatic "people like you" (Greek hymeis) carries contempt.
orig: ἐν ποίῳ ὀνόματι (en poiō onomati)

p: The Spirit fills Peter for this moment, as Jesus had promised for trials before rulers.
b: Jesus had told his disciples that when they were brought before synagogues and rulers, they should not worry about what to say, "for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you must say" (Luke 12:11–12; compare Luke 21:12–15). Luke uses "filled with the Holy Spirit" (plēstheis, aorist) for a fresh empowering for a task (2:4; 4:31; 13:9), and "full of the Spirit" (plērēs) for a lasting character (6:3, 5; 11:24). So Peter, filled at Pentecost, is filled again for the trial.
orig: πλησθεὶς πνεύματος ἁγίου (plēstheis pneumatos hagiou)

a: by what means this man has been saved
p: The verb sōzō means both "heal" and "save." Peter moves from the man's healing to salvation for all in 4:12.
b: In the Gospels sōzō is used of healing ("your faith has saved you," Luke 8:48), and this translation keeps "saved" so that the reader can follow Peter's argument. The lame man "has been saved" (4:9), made whole by Jesus' name; so "there is no salvation in anyone else" (4:12), the noun from the same root. The physical healing is a sign of the larger rescue Jesus brings. The word for "kindness" (euergesia) was a word for public benefactions: Peter points out the oddity of a trial for doing someone good.
orig: ἐν τίνι οὗτος σέσωται (en tini houtos sesōtai)

a: the stone that you, the builders, treated as nothing
p: Psalm 118:22, a favorite early Christian text. Peter addresses the builders directly: "you."
b: "A stone that the builders threw out / has become the head of the corner" (Psalm 118:22). Jesus quoted it at the end of the parable of the vineyard, aimed at the chief priests and scribes (Luke 20:17), and 1 Peter 2:7 uses it again. Peter does not quote the Greek Psalm exactly: he uses a sharper verb, exoutheneō, "treat with contempt, count as nothing," the word Luke uses for Herod treating Jesus with contempt (Luke 23:11), and he turns the Psalm into a direct charge, "you, the builders." The "head of the corner" is either the cornerstone at the foundation or the capstone at the top of an arch or wall.
orig: ὁ λίθος ὁ ἐξουθενηθεὶς ὑφ᾽ ὑμῶν τῶν οἰκοδόμων (ho lithos ho exouthenētheis hyph' hymōn tōn oikodomōn)
r: Psalm 118:22; Luke 20:17–18; Luke 23:11; Matthew 21:42; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Isaiah 28:16

a: there is no salvation in anyone else
p: Christians agree Jesus is the only Savior. They differ on whether people who never hear his name can be saved.
b: Exclusivist reading: salvation comes only through Jesus, and only to those who hear of him and believe; many evangelicals hold this (the Lausanne Covenant 3 cites this verse). Inclusivist reading: salvation comes only through Christ, but God may save some who do not know his name, through Christ's work and grace given in ways known to God; this is Catholic teaching (Lumen Gentium 16) and the view of many Orthodox and Protestants (Karl Rahner's "anonymous Christians" is one form). Pluralist reading: some modern theologians, such as John Hick, hold that the great religions are different paths to the same reality, and read the verse as the language of devotion rather than a claim about others. In its setting, Peter speaks to Israel's leaders about the name in which the lame man was healed.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἄλλῳ οὐδενὶ ἡ σωτηρία (ouk estin en allō oudeni hē sōtēria)

a: these men had no schooling and held no office
p: Not trained under the scribes, and private men without official standing. Not "illiterate."
b: Agrammatos literally means "without letters," but here it most likely means without formal training in the Scriptures under a recognized teacher, as the scribes had (compare John 7:15, of Jesus). Idiōtēs is a private person, a layman, someone without office (it gave English "idiot," but did not mean that). Fishermen in Galilee could likely read some Hebrew or Aramaic, and many knew some Greek. The council is surprised that such men argue from Scripture so freely, and they recognize the cause: "these two had been Jesus' companions."
orig: ἀγράμματοί ... καὶ ἰδιῶται (agrammatoi ... kai idiōtai)

p: Parrēsia: freedom of speech, the citizen's right to speak openly. A key word in Acts 4.
b: In Greek cities parrēsia was the citizen's freedom to say anything, and then courage to speak frankly before the powerful. It appears three times in this chapter (4:13, 29, 31) and closes the whole book: Paul preaching "with complete freedom to speak, and no one stopped him" (28:31). This translation says "freely" where the plain sense is open speech, and adds "courage" or "fearlessly" where danger is present (4:29, 31). What the council sees as nerve, the believers pray for as a gift (4:29), and God answers (4:31).
orig: τὴν τοῦ Πέτρου παρρησίαν (tēn tou Petrou parrēsian)

p: Greek synedrion, "council," borrowed into Hebrew and Aramaic as sanhedrin.
b: Synedrion means a council or court, literally "sitting together." Jews took the Greek word into Hebrew as sanhedrin, and this translation uses that name for the high council in Jerusalem, as the site's Matthew does (Matthew 26:59). The apostles appear before it again in chapter 5, Stephen in chapter 6, and Paul in chapter 23. How the Christians knew what was said in the closed session (4:15–17) is not stated; some suggest sympathizers such as Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea or, later, Paul.
orig: τοῦ συνεδρίου (tou synedriou)

a: a well-known sign has happened through them
p: The council does not dispute the healing. They dispute what it means and who may speak of it.
b: Luke stresses that the opponents admit the facts (compare John 11:47, "The man is doing many signs"). The issue is control: the council wants the news to stop spreading "among the people" (4:17). Ancient readers knew the argument from silence and the argument from enemies: when opponents concede a point, it is strong evidence. Luke uses this kind of argument often; Paul tells King Agrippa that these things did not happen in a corner (26:26).

a: Is it right before God to heed you rather than God
t: Obeying God rather than human rulers
p: A principle of civil disobedience that echoes Socrates and the Jewish martyrs. It returns in 5:29.
b: Peter and John answer in words close to those Plato gives Socrates at his trial: "I will obey the god rather than you" (Apology 29d), and educated readers would have caught the echo. The Jewish martyrs of the Maccabean revolt said the same about the king's commands (2 Maccabees 7:2, 30). Christians have appealed to this verse and to 5:29 in every age, from refusing to offer incense to the emperor to resisting unjust laws, while also teaching submission to governing authorities (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). The traditions differ on when disobedience is allowed; see the topic page.
r: 5:29; Daniel 3:16–18; Daniel 6:10; 2 Maccabees 7:2; 2 Maccabees 7:30; Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17

p: The man had been lame for over forty years, so there was no doubt about the miracle.
b: Luke adds the detail at the end of the story to stress that the healing was beyond question. Some readers note the number forty, Israel's years in the wilderness, but Luke does not draw any symbol from it. The council's helplessness (4:21) comes from the people, who had all seen him lame for decades and now saw him walk.

p: Despotēs: the lord of a household with full authority over slaves. The believers call themselves his slaves (4:29).
b: Despotēs is used for God in Jewish prayers in Greek (Judith 9:12; 2 Maccabees 15:22; Wisdom 6:7) and by Simeon in Luke 2:29 ("Master, now you are setting your slave free"). It stresses God's total rule over creation and history, the theme of the prayer: he made heaven, earth and sea, and even the plotting of rulers fell within what his hand had marked out (4:28). The words "heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them" echo Exodus 20:11, Nehemiah 9:6 and Psalm 146:6.
orig: Δέσποτα (Despota)

a: Through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of your servant David, our father
p: The Greek of this line is notoriously tangled; the later manuscripts smoothed it out.
b: The best manuscripts read, word for word, "who of our father through the Holy Spirit mouth of David your servant saying," which is hard to construe. Bruce Metzger discusses it as one of the hardest readings in Acts, and scholars have suggested an early copying error or an Aramaic phrase behind it. The Byzantine text (and the KJV) has the simpler "who by the mouth of your servant David said." The sense is clear in either form: God spoke through David by the Spirit, as in 1:16. See the variant.
orig: ὁ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου στόματος Δαυὶδ παιδός σου εἰπών

p: A royal psalm about nations plotting against God's anointed king. The church reads it of Jesus' trial.
b: Psalm 2 pictures kings and rulers plotting "against the LORD and against his anointed one" (Psalm 2:2), and God installing his king on Zion and calling him "my son" (Psalm 2:6–7). The believers quote the Greek Psalm, then match each part to the passion (4:27): the "kings" are Herod Antipas, the "rulers" Pontius Pilate, the "nations" the Gentiles (the Roman soldiers), and the "peoples" the people of Israel. In Jewish tradition the psalm was read of the king and later of the Messiah (Psalms of Solomon 17:23–24 borrows its language); Paul applies Psalm 2:7 to Jesus' resurrection (13:33).
r: Psalm 2:1–2; Psalm 2:7; 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Revelation 19:15; Psalms of Solomon 17:23–24

p: The Greek christos means "anointed one." The next verse plays on it: Jesus, "whom you anointed."
b: The site's Psalm 2:2 reads "against the LORD and against his anointed one" from the Hebrew meshicho. The Greek christos means the same, and this translation says "his Messiah" because Acts uses the word as the title of Jesus. The prayer then says that God "anointed" (echrisas) Jesus (4:27), which ties the title to his baptism, when the Spirit came on him (Luke 3:22; 4:18, "he anointed me"; Acts 10:38).
orig: κατὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ (kata tou christou autou)

p: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, and Pontius Pilate, Rome's governor of Judea. Only Luke tells of Jesus before Herod.
b: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39; Luke alone tells how Pilate sent Jesus to him and how the two became friends that day (Luke 23:6–12). Pontius Pilate was prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36; an inscription naming him was found at Caesarea in 1961. In Luke's Gospel both rulers find Jesus not guilty (Luke 23:14–15), yet both share in his death, as the Psalm said rulers would gather against the anointed one.

a: your hand and your purpose had marked out ahead of time
p: The verb proorizō, "decide beforehand, predestine." The church's prayer sees God's plan in the crucifixion.
b: Proorizō is the word Paul uses for God's predestining (Romans 8:29–30; Ephesians 1:5, 11). Here it is not about who will be saved but about the events of the passion: what the rulers did freely and wickedly was what God's "hand," his power, and his "purpose" had decided would happen. This is the same tension as 2:23, held without explanation; see the note there.
orig: προώρισεν γενέσθαι (proōrisen genesthai)

a: Let your slaves speak your word
p: They do not ask for safety or for their enemies to be punished, but for courage to keep speaking.
b: The prayer asks God to "see" the threats, as Hezekiah asked God to look at the Assyrian king's insulting message (Isaiah 37:17). But the request is not for protection: it is for parrēsia, bold freedom of speech (4:13), and for God to keep healing and doing signs through Jesus' name. The believers call themselves God's "slaves" (douloi), the word of Joel's prophecy in 2:18. The answer comes at once (4:31).
orig: δὸς τοῖς δούλοις σου μετὰ παρρησίας πάσης λαλεῖν (dos tois doulois sou meta parrēsias pasēs lalein)

a: the place where they had gathered shook
p: In the Old Testament the earth shakes when God comes near. This is a sign that the prayer was heard.
b: When God came down at Sinai "the whole mountain quaked hard" (Exodus 19:18), and when Isaiah saw the LORD, "the bases of the doorways trembled" (Isaiah 6:4). Greek and Roman readers also took an earthquake as a sign of a god's answer. At Philippi an earthquake frees Paul and Silas while they pray and sing (16:25–26). The shaking here is followed by a new filling with the Spirit, which some call "a little Pentecost."

p: A Jewish phrase for complete unity, and a Greek proverb for friendship: "one soul in two bodies."
b: Deuteronomy speaks of loving God with all one's heart and being (Deuteronomy 6:5), and 1 Chronicles 12:38 says all Israel "was of one heart to make David king." Greek writers defined friends as "one soul" (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 9.8, quotes the saying with "friends' things are common"). Luke joins the Jewish and the Greek ideals: the believers are one in heart, and their goods are common. Augustine opened his Rule for monks with this verse.
orig: καρδία καὶ ψυχὴ μία (kardia kai psychē mia)

a: rich grace rested on all of them
p: Charis can mean God's favor or the people's goodwill. Both fit, since 2:47 says the believers had the people's favor.
b: Charis is the gift of kindness that no one earned, God's grace; but it also means the favor people show someone, as in 2:47, where the believers "were well liked by all the people" (literally "having favor with all the people"). Luke said of the boy Jesus that he grew "in favor with God and with people" (Luke 2:52). Most readers take this as God's grace at work among the believers, which the next verse shows in action: no one is in need.
orig: χάρις τε μεγάλη (charis te megalē)

a: Nobody among them was in need
p: Moses' promise for Israel in the land, "there will be no one in need among you," comes true in the church.
b: Deuteronomy 15:4 says, "Yet there will be no one in need among you," in the law about cancelling debts every seventh year, and adds that this depends on Israel obeying (Deuteronomy 15:5); yet Deuteronomy 15:11 admits, "there will never stop being people in need in the land." The Greek of Deuteronomy uses the same rare word as Acts, endeēs, "needy." Luke presents the believers as the restored people of God, living out the Law's ideal. Ancient readers might also hear the Greek dream of a golden age when all was shared.
orig: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐνδεής τις ἦν ἐν αὐτοῖς (oude gar endeēs tis ēn en autois)

a: placed it at the feet of the apostles
p: Laying something at a person's feet was a sign of handing it over to his authority.
b: The phrase comes three times (4:35, 37; 5:2), and Luke uses the same gesture for submission in other stories (Luke 7:38; 8:35, 41; 10:39). The apostles control the common fund, which later becomes too much for them, leading to the appointment of the Seven (6:1–6). Placing a gift at their feet also prepares for the contrast in 5:1–2, where Ananias brings only part.

p: A Levite from the large Jewish community on Cyprus. He will become Paul's partner.
b: Levites served in the temple as assistants to the priests. Numbers 18:20–24 says the Levites were to have no inheritance of land, but by this time Levites, like priests, could own property (Jeremiah, a priest, bought a field, Jeremiah 32:6–15). Cyprus had many Jews (Josephus, Antiquities 13.284; 1 Maccabees 15:23). Barnabas is the bridge to the rest of Acts: he vouches for Paul in Jerusalem (9:27), leads the church at Antioch (11:22–26), and travels with Paul (13:2–15:39). His cousin was John Mark (Colossians 4:10).

p: Luke's translation of the nickname Barnabas. The Aramaic behind it is uncertain.
b: "Son of" in Hebrew and Aramaic names a person by a quality. Luke explains Barnabas as huios paraklēseōs; paraklēsis means encouragement, comfort or exhortation, related to paraklētos, "Advocate" (John 14:16). Scholars have struggled to derive this from Aramaic: bar nabya', "son of a prophet" (prophecy includes encouragement, 15:32), is a common suggestion; another links it to a Semitic name Bar-Nebo. Whatever the origin, Barnabas lives up to the name (11:23).
orig: υἱὸς παρακλήσεως (huios paraklēseōs)
